slides.headline: A big cat that does not roar.
slides.sub: Meet the snow leopard, the quiet one of the mountains

slides.headline: No roar, just a yowl
slides.body: Unlike other big cats, snow leopards do not roar. They yowl to advertise where they are, and greet each other with a soft, nasal chuff.

slides.headline: Some roaring parts, not all
slides.body: It has the partly elastic hyoid of roaring cats, once credited for the roar. But its vocal folds are only intermediate between roarers and other cats.
slides.source: Weissengruber et al., Journal of Anatomy (2002)

slides.headline: A tail almost as long as its body
slides.body: At 80–100 cm (75–90% of its body length), the tail aids balance on steep rock and covers its extremities in harsh winter weather.

slides.headline: Built for thin air
slides.body: Found from about 500 to 5,800 m, mostly at 3,000–4,500 m, across 12 countries including India, Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan.
slides.source: IUCN Red List (2016); Animal Diversity Web

slides.headline: Vulnerable, and still declining
slides.body: The IUCN (assessed 2016) estimates 2,710–3,386 mature snow leopards, with a decreasing trend. Threats include hunting, livestock farming, mining, roads and climate change.

caption:
The snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a big cat that does not roar. It yowls, chuffs and stays out of sight.

Snow leopards share the partly elastic hyoid bone that was long thought to explain roaring, yet their vocal folds differ from those of lions and tigers. Between 1986 and 2017 the species was listed as Endangered, then moved to Vulnerable after a calculation error was found in the 2008 population assessment.

Swipe for the yowl, the tail and the numbers. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List (Panthera uncia, assessed 2016); Animal Diversity Web; Weissengruber et al. (2002), Journal of Anatomy; Britannica.
